--- title: "Poisson Regression via MLE: Blueprinty Case" author: "Tweety Chang" date: 2025-05-07 date-format: "MMMM YYYY" description: "Count-data model estimated by maximum likelihood: software customers show ~23% more patents after controlling for firm age and region." categories: [Statistical Modeling] image: figures/fig4_predicted_patents.png callout-appearance: minimal --- ::: {.biz-value} ### Adjusted Association - **Question:** Do engineering firms that use Blueprinty's software earn more patents, once firm age and region are taken into account? - **Approach:** Derived the Poisson likelihood, maximized it by hand, and confirmed the result against statsmodels. Then tested the finding under overdispersion with robust standard errors and a negative binomial model. - **Finding:** Customers have about **23% more expected patents** (incidence rate ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.15–1.32 across all three specifications), or about **0.8 more patents per firm** over five years. - **Caveat:** Customers were not randomly assigned, so this is an adjusted association, not proof that the software causes more patents. ::: ## The Question Blueprinty, a fictional company in this case study, sells software that helps firms prepare patent applications. Its marketing team wants evidence that customers are more successful at getting patents. Approval rates before and after adoption are not available. What is available is a cross-section of 1,500 mature engineering firms: patents awarded over the last five years, region, firm age, and whether the firm uses Blueprinty. The analysis asks whether customers earn more patents after accounting for age and region, and how confident that conclusion can be. ## Data ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Data dictionary"} | Variable | Description | |:--------------|:------------| | `patents` | Number of patents awarded in the last 5 years (count outcome) | | `region` | Midwest, Northeast, Northwest, South, or Southwest | | `age` | Years since incorporation | | `iscustomer` | 1 = Blueprinty customer, 0 = non-customer | ::: Customers average **4.13** patents over five years versus **3.47** for non-customers. That raw gap cannot be taken at face value, because customers differ from non-customers in ways that may also affect patenting. **Figure 1. Distribution of patent counts by Blueprinty usage** ![Distribution of patent counts by Blueprinty usage](figures/fig1_blueprinty_patent_hist.png){#fig-blueprinty-hist} Patent counts are right-skewed, as count data usually are, and customers sit modestly further right. **Firm age by customer status** | Customer | Firms | Mean age | Median age | SD | |---------:|------:|---------:|-----------:|---:| | No | 1,019 | 26.10 | 25.50 | 6.95 | | Yes | 481 | 26.90 | 26.50 | 7.81 | **Region by customer status** | Region | Non-customers | Customers | Total | |-----------|-----:|-----:|------:| | Midwest | 187 | 37 | 224 | | Northeast | 273 | 328 | 601 | | Northwest | 158 | 29 | 187 | | South | 156 | 35 | 191 | | Southwest | 245 | 52 | 297 | | Total | 1,019 | 481 | 1,500 | Age is similar across groups, but region is not: **68% of customers are in the Northeast**, where most non-customers are not. Both variables are therefore controlled for in the model. ## A Baseline Poisson Model Because patents are non-negative counts, the natural starting point is $Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$. For $n$ independent firms the log-likelihood is $$ \ell(\lambda) = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\right)\log\lambda - \sum_{i=1}^n \log(y_i!). $$ Setting the derivative $-n + \sum y_i / \lambda$ to zero gives $\hat\lambda = \bar y$. Numerically maximizing the likelihood confirms it: $\hat\lambda = 3.6847 = \bar y$. **Figure 2. Poisson log-likelihood across values of λ** ![Poisson log-likelihood across values of lambda](figures/fig2_poisson_loglik_vs_lambda.png){#fig-poisson-loglik} ## Poisson Regression To compare firms on equal terms, each firm gets its own rate: $$ Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad \log \lambda_i = X_i^\top \beta, $$ where $X_i$ contains customer status, age, age squared, and region indicators (Midwest as the reference). **Checking the hand-written likelihood.** Maximizing the custom log-likelihood with BFGS reproduces the statsmodels GLM estimates to four decimal places, which confirms the implementation. Age is centered here to keep the optimization well-conditioned. ::: {#d43ff2df .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
Hand-written MLE statsmodels GLM
const 1.3447 1.3447
age_c -0.0080 -0.0080
age_c2 -0.0030 -0.0030
iscustomer 0.2076 0.2076
region_Northeast 0.0292 0.0292
region_Northwest -0.0176 -0.0176
region_South 0.0566 0.0566
region_Southwest 0.0506 0.0506
``` ::: ::: **Results (uncentered age)** | Term | Estimate | Std. Error | z | p-value | 95% CI | |------|---------:|-----------:|--:|--------:|:------:| | Intercept | −0.5089 | 0.1832 | −2.78 | 0.006 | −0.868 to −0.150 | | age | 0.1486 | 0.0139 | 10.72 | <0.001 | 0.121 to 0.176 | | age² | −0.0030 | 0.0003 | −11.51 | <0.001 | −0.0035 to −0.0025 | | **iscustomer** | **0.2076** | 0.0309 | 6.72 | <0.001 | 0.147 to 0.268 | | Northeast | 0.0292 | 0.0436 | 0.67 | 0.504 | −0.056 to 0.115 | | Northwest | −0.0176 | 0.0538 | −0.33 | 0.744 | −0.123 to 0.088 | | South | 0.0566 | 0.0527 | 1.07 | 0.283 | −0.047 to 0.160 | | Southwest | 0.0506 | 0.0472 | 1.07 | 0.284 | −0.042 to 0.143 | *Coefficients are on the log scale; exp(coefficient) is the incidence rate ratio (IRR).* - **Customers:** exp(0.2076) = 1.23, so customers have about 23% more expected patents than otherwise similar non-customers. - **Age:** the positive age term and negative age² term put the peak at about **25 years** (0.1486 / (2 × 0.0030)). Expected patents rise for younger firms and fall for older ones. - **Region:** no region differs significantly from the Midwest once age and customer status are included. The Northeast's high raw patent count reflects its concentration of customers. **Figure 3. Coefficients with 95% confidence intervals** ![Poisson regression coefficients with 95% confidence intervals](figures/fig3_poisson_coef_plot.png){#fig-poisson-coefs} ## Robustness A Poisson model assumes the variance equals the mean. Here the Pearson statistic is about 1.39 times its degrees of freedom, so the data are mildly overdispersed and the plain Poisson standard errors are too small. Two standard fixes, robust (sandwich) standard errors and a negative binomial model, leave the conclusion unchanged: ::: {#15a56455 .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson chi-square / df = 2072.7 / 1492 = 1.39; negative binomial alpha = 0.092 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
Coefficient Std. error IRR IRR 95% CI
Poisson 0.2076 0.0309 1.231 1.158 – 1.308
Poisson, robust SE 0.2076 0.0352 1.231 1.149 – 1.319
Negative binomial 0.2073 0.0361 1.23 1.146 – 1.321
``` ::: ::: The customer effect stays at an IRR of 1.23 in every specification, and the widest interval (negative binomial) still runs from about 1.15 to 1.32. ## What It Means **Figure 4. Predicted five-year patents by firm age (Midwest)** ![Predicted patents by Blueprinty usage](figures/fig4_predicted_patents.png){#fig-predicted-patents} ::: {#c6434db1 .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Average predicted patents: 3.44 as non-customers vs 4.23 as customers (+0.79 per firm over five years) ``` ::: ::: Because the effect is multiplicative, the absolute gap is largest where patenting peaks, around age 25. Across the actual firms in the data, switching every firm to customer status raises predicted output by about 0.8 patents over five years. ## Limitations and Next Steps - **Selection, not causation.** Firms chose to buy the software. More productive or better-funded firms may be the ones that buy, which would inflate the estimate. Adoption timing, or a before-and-after panel, would allow a difference-in-differences design. - **Omitted variables.** Firm size, R&D spending, and industry are not in the data and could explain part of the gap. - **Outcome definition.** Patents awarded is not the same as approval rate, which is what Blueprinty actually wants to claim. - **Recommendation for Blueprinty.** The data support a careful claim ("customers earn about 23% more patents than comparable firms"), not a causal one ("our software increases patents by 23%").
